title: Episode 11: VS Code Setup and Accessibility
description: Screen reader mode, Command Palette, sidebar navigation, and accessibility settings.
concepts: What VS Code is: a free, extensible code editor by Microsoft
The github.dev experience: press . on any repo to open VS Code in the browser
Screen reader mode: what it enables and how to turn it on
The accessibility help dialog: Control+Shift+H (what it tells you)
The Command Palette: Control+Shift+P - the most important shortcut
The Activity Bar: Explorer, Search, Source Control, Extensions, etc.
Navigating between the sidebar, editor, terminal, and panels
The integrated terminal and how to open it
Opening a folder versus opening a file
Installing extensions from the Extensions view
Key accessibility settings: editor.accessibilitySupport, screen reader announcements
Audio cues and what they signal
The accessible diff viewer (Accessible Diff Viewer in Command Palette)
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're getting your editing environment ready in a way that actually works for blind and low-vision contributors. We're focusing on VS Code: how to access it, how to make it screen-reader friendly, how to sign in to GitHub, how to check whether Copilot is available, and how to move around the interface without guessing.

[JAMIE]
And I like that this is framed as setup, not as a side quest. Because if your editor is confusing or inaccessible, everything after that gets harder.

[ALEX]
Exactly. This is foundation work. And there's one practical note right up front: there's a related audio overview for this material along with the next chapter, there are supporting appendices for VS Code reference and screen reader shortcuts, and the most authoritative references are the VS Code documentation on user interface and accessibility.

[JAMIE]
So if a learner wants both the workshop explanation and the official product docs, they should use both.

[ALEX]
Yes. Also, this is Day 2, Block 1 material, and it assumes you've already done the Day 1 walkthrough in GitHub's browser interface. That matters, because VS Code makes more sense once GitHub.com itself feels familiar.

[JAMIE]
What are we actually trying to be able to do by the end?

[ALEX]
Launch VS Code, either in the browser with github.dev or on the desktop app, turn on screen reader support, sign in to GitHub, verify whether Copilot is active, and confidently move through the main interface areas like Explorer, the status bar, menus, settings, and keyboard shortcuts.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
For this workshop, this is a guided setup chapter with one lightweight completion practice. There isn't an automated check, because setup state lives on your device and account. So instead, your evidence is a structured completion comment on your assigned challenge issue.

[JAMIE]
So the pattern here is: open, configure, navigate, verify.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The single practice is your accessibility baseline. You open VS Code in github.dev or desktop, enable screen reader mode, sign in to GitHub, check Copilot status, and navigate core surfaces.

[JAMIE]
Let's walk through that like we're doing it together.

[ALEX]
Start on your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com. Then press the period key. Just a plain dot. On a repository code page, that launches github.dev, which is a browser-based version of VS Code. Give it a few seconds to load.

[JAMIE]
And if pressing period does nothing?

[ALEX]
That usually means you aren't on the repository's main code page. Maybe you're inside an issue or pull request. The shortcut works on repository code pages.

[JAMIE]
Once github.dev opens, accessibility comes first, right?

[ALEX]
Always. On Windows with NVDA or JAWS, press Shift+Alt+F1 to enable screen reader mode. You should hear an announcement confirming it. On Mac with VoiceOver, the environment is often already reasonably optimized, but if navigation feels off, open the Command Palette with Command+Shift+P and run the command called Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode.

[JAMIE]
Then Explorer?

[ALEX]
Yes. Open Explorer with Control+Shift+E on Windows or Command+Shift+E on Mac. Your screen reader should announce the file tree. Use the arrow keys to move through files, find README.md, and press Enter to open it.

[JAMIE]
And then there's a really useful navigation trick for long Markdown files.

[ALEX]
Right: outline or symbols. Press Control+Shift+O, or Command+Shift+O on Mac. In a Markdown file, that gives you headings and sections. For screen reader users, that becomes one of the fastest ways to jump around a document.

[JAMIE]
Then the Command Palette.

[ALEX]
Open it with Control+Shift+P or Command+Shift+P. Type a command, like Toggle Word Wrap, and run it. Or press Escape to back out. The key idea is that the Command Palette gives you keyboard access to nearly everything in VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And after that we verify account and tool state.

[ALEX]
Yes. Find the Accounts button, which is typically near the bottom left area of the interface. If you're signed in, your screen reader should announce your GitHub username. If not, activate it and sign in. Then check the status bar at the bottom and move through it to look for GitHub Copilot status.

[JAMIE]
Though there's a catch there.

[ALEX]
There is. github.dev does not support Copilot the same way desktop VS Code does. So if you don't find Copilot in github.dev, that may be expected. Desktop VS Code or a Codespace is where Copilot support is more complete.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What counts as done for the practice?

[ALEX]
You're done when you've opened github.dev, enabled screen reader mode, signed in to GitHub, checked Copilot status, opened a file, viewed its outline, and run a command from the Command Palette.

[JAMIE]
And then comes the evidence comment.

[ALEX]
Yes. Go back to GitHub.com, open your assigned setup or readiness issue, and post a completion comment listing whether you opened github.dev, enabled screen reader mode, signed in to GitHub, checked Copilot status, opened a file in Explorer, opened outline or symbols, and opened the Command Palette. If any answer is no, add a note about where you got stuck. Then close the assigned setup or readiness issue.

[JAMIE]
That's helpful because it turns setup into something visible, not vague.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The expected outcomes are practical: you can launch and navigate github.dev or desktop VS Code, you can hear navigation announcements, you're signed in to GitHub, you've verified Copilot or understand its limitations, you can open Explorer, Outline, and Command Palette, and you're ready for the VS Code-based chapters that follow.

[JAMIE]
Can we pause on the "if you get stuck" moments? Because those are often the real lesson.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. If the period key does nothing, check that you're on the repository page. If the screen reader toggle didn't announce anything, use the Command Palette and search for screen reader commands manually. If Explorer seems empty, the repository may still be loading, so wait a few seconds and try again. If VoiceOver navigation feels wrong, explicitly run the screen reader mode toggle. If you can't find the Accounts button, use the Command Palette and search for Accounts. If Copilot isn't in the status bar, remember github.dev may not support it. If a shortcut fails, the Command Palette is your fallback. And if needed, ask a facilitator for a side-by-side demo and repeat the same steps.

[JAMIE]
That last part matters. Repetition is not failure. It's skill-building.

[ALEX]
Exactly. There's also a learning moment here: tool setup is part of contribution skill. A stable, accessible editor reduces stress and improves the quality of your work. And the specific things you just tested are not random. github.dev launch, screen reader mode, GitHub sign-in, Copilot status, Explorer, Outline, and Command Palette are the foundation for the rest of the workflow.

[JAMIE]
And there's also a reusable learning pattern.

[ALEX]
Yes: open the tool in the simplest way possible, sign in and verify your identity and tools, configure accessibility before doing any work, verify each navigation surface with assistive tech, and record what worked and what didn't.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's answer the bigger question: why use VS Code at all if GitHub's website already lets you do a lot?

[ALEX]
Because GitHub's browser interface is excellent for reviewing, discussing, and triaging, while VS Code is where you create. On GitHub.com, navigating repositories, reading issues and pull requests, and leaving comments are all very strong. But when you need full editing, richer navigation, live feedback, AI assistance, and tighter Git workflows, VS Code becomes the better workspace.

[JAMIE]
So for editing Markdown contributions, which is a lot of open source contribution work, VS Code gives you a stronger environment.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You get a real text editor, live preview, Copilot assistance when supported, and less tab switching. You also get earlier feedback. Instead of finding out after you push that something is wrong, you can often hear or see errors while you type.

[JAMIE]
And for screen reader users, that immediate feedback is huge.

[ALEX]
It is. One of the important ideas in the learning cards is that VS Code can announce errors, warnings, and suggestions through accessibility mechanisms like ARIA live regions. That means you don't have to wait until a change reaches GitHub to discover a problem. Also, the Command Palette gives you a universal keyboard entry point to features, and the Explorer sidebar gives you a repository tree similar to GitHub.com, but tuned for editing.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before installing anything, there's this bridge tool: github.dev.

[ALEX]
Yes. Think of github.dev as VS Code in your browser. It lets you try the VS Code interface immediately, inside a repository, without committing to a desktop install first.

[JAMIE]
That makes it a gentle on-ramp.

[ALEX]
Exactly. There are three main ways to access it. The fastest is pressing the period key while you're on a repository page. That works on repository code pages. Another method is using the direct URL form by changing a GitHub repository URL to the github.dev version. And another is launching it from the repository page interface itself.

[JAMIE]
What do you get when it opens?

[ALEX]
You get a full VS Code-style editor in the browser: file explorer, editor tabs, command palette, settings, and the overall interface model you'll later use in desktop VS Code. It's excellent for orientation, small edits, navigation practice, and learning the environment.

[JAMIE]
And what does it not have?

[ALEX]
It does not give you the full desktop experience. Some features are limited or missing, especially ones that rely on local tooling or deeper extension support. And, importantly for this workshop, Copilot support is not the same there. So github.dev is a bridge, not a complete replacement.

[JAMIE]
So when should learners use github.dev, and when should they switch to desktop VS Code?

[ALEX]
Use github.dev when you want the simplest possible start, when you're learning the interface, when you need quick edits, or when you want to confirm you can navigate the environment before installing anything. Use desktop VS Code when you need richer features, more complete extension support, stronger Git integration, and tools like Copilot in the ways the workshop expects.

[JAMIE]
Let's make the screen reader experience in github.dev explicit.

[ALEX]
Good idea. In github.dev, activate screen reader mode immediately. Don't wait until navigation feels broken. Once it's on, VS Code changes how it presents and announces interface elements to work better with assistive technology. Navigation becomes more predictable, announcements become more informative, and moving among panes, trees, editors, and controls makes more sense.

[JAMIE]
Anything platform-specific there?

[ALEX]
Yes. NVDA and JAWS users on Windows should use the direct keyboard toggle when available and listen for confirmation. VoiceOver users on Mac may find things mostly optimized already, but if behavior seems inconsistent, explicitly toggling screen reader accessibility mode through the Command Palette often improves the experience.

[JAMIE]
And there's a "try it right now" spirit to this whole section.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Don't just hear about github.dev. Open a repository, press period, enable accessibility mode, and move around. The fastest way to reduce mystery is direct contact.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's broaden from github.dev to VS Code generally. What is screen reader mode in VS Code actually doing?

[ALEX]
Screen reader mode is VS Code's accessibility layer for nonvisual navigation and feedback. It changes how the app exposes information, how much is announced, and how certain interactions are presented so screen readers can work more effectively.

[JAMIE]
How do learners activate it?

[ALEX]
On Windows, a common shortcut is Shift+Alt+F1. On any platform, you can always open the Command Palette and search for the command to toggle screen reader accessibility mode. That fallback matters because shortcuts can vary by setup.

[JAMIE]
And how do you verify it's active?

[ALEX]
Listen for the confirmation announcement. Then test something concrete: open Explorer, move through a tree, switch focus between interface regions, or navigate a file outline. If those interactions become clearer and more consistently announced, that's a strong sign it's on.

[JAMIE]
What changes once the mode is active?

[ALEX]
VS Code becomes much more intentional about accessibility output. Focus changes are clearer, tree views and lists are easier to interpret, announcements provide more context, and in general the editor behaves more like a well-structured application rather than a visually optimized one that a screen reader is trying to interpret after the fact.

[JAMIE]
The source also calls out platform-specific settings. What should learners take from that?

[ALEX]
That accessibility is not one-size-fits-all. NVDA users may need settings that reduce friction with browse mode or improve spoken feedback in VS Code. JAWS users may have their own preferred interaction patterns and may benefit from explicitly confirming how virtual cursor behavior interacts with the app. VoiceOver users on macOS may need to verify the screen reader mode toggle and adapt to Mac-specific focus conventions. The deeper point is: tune VS Code to your screen reader, not just to generic defaults.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's do the interface tour. If someone opens VS Code and feels overwhelmed, what should they picture first?

[ALEX]
Picture five major regions. First, the activity bar or primary navigation area that gives quick access to views like Explorer and Search. Second, the side bar, where the selected view's content appears, such as the file tree in Explorer. Third, the editor area, where your files open and where you do most writing and editing. Fourth, panels or auxiliary areas that can show things like output or other tools, depending on configuration. And fifth, the status bar along the bottom, which reports state and provides quick-access controls.

[JAMIE]
That already makes it less scary. Not a thousand mystery elements, just a few major zones.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Once learners understand the regions, navigation becomes purposeful. You aren't wandering. You're moving from region to region.

[JAMIE]
So how do you navigate between regions efficiently?

[ALEX]
Use direct shortcuts whenever possible. Explorer has a shortcut. The Command Palette has a shortcut. Outline or symbols has a shortcut. Menus can be reached from the keyboard. Settings and keyboard shortcuts have commands. Screen reader users often do best when they rely on known jumps instead of trying to tab through every control in order.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card idea here is basically: know the landmarks.

[ALEX]
Yes. Find your way around by learning the interface landmarks and a few dependable shortcuts. Once you know where Explorer, the editor, status bar, accounts area, and menus live conceptually, VS Code becomes much less cognitively heavy.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Speaking of identity and setup, let's talk about the Accounts button and signing in to GitHub.

[ALEX]
This matters because many GitHub-connected features in VS Code depend on authentication. Signing in connects your editor to your GitHub account so repository actions, account-aware features, and tools tied to your identity can work smoothly.

[JAMIE]
How do you sign in?

[ALEX]
One path is through the Accounts button in the lower-left area. Activate it, choose the GitHub sign-in option, and follow the browser-based authorization flow. Another path is through the Command Palette: search for sign-in or accounts-related commands and launch the sign-in flow from there.

[JAMIE]
How do you verify that it worked?

[ALEX]
Return to the Accounts control and listen for your GitHub username, or otherwise confirm that the interface now reflects your signed-in state. The important thing is to verify, not assume.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card summary would be: sign-in is not decorative. It unlocks the account-connected workflow.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Next up: GitHub Copilot status. This is one of those features learners hear about a lot, but they're often unsure whether it's actually on.

[ALEX]
That's why verification matters. There are three good ways to check. First, the status bar may include a Copilot indicator. Second, the Command Palette may show Copilot commands, which is another clue that the feature is installed and available. Third, a quick test in an editable file may reveal whether suggestions are appearing.

[JAMIE]
And if it's not working?

[ALEX]
Troubleshoot systematically. Confirm you're signed in to the correct GitHub account. Confirm you're in an environment that supports Copilot, usually desktop VS Code rather than github.dev. Check whether the extension or feature is present and enabled. If the status bar doesn't mention it and commands aren't showing, you may not have the supported environment or active setup yet.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card here is basically: don't guess based on marketing. Check actual indicators.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's spend a moment on the status bar itself, because beginners often ignore it.

[ALEX]
And they shouldn't. The status bar is one of VS Code's most useful summary surfaces. Left to right, it can contain source control or branch information, sync and environment indicators, encoding or line-ending details, language mode, position in the file, accessibility-related state, extension indicators, and sometimes GitHub-connected status such as Copilot.

[JAMIE]
So it's not just decorative chrome. It's operational information.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And for keyboard users, you should practice navigating it intentionally. Use keyboard movement to enter it and move across its items. The point is to learn that important state lives there and can be accessed without a mouse.

[JAMIE]
This seems especially useful for low-vision users too, because the status bar often centralizes tiny but important details.

[ALEX]
Yes. It's a compact dashboard. Learn to consult it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now the menu bar. Some people come to VS Code expecting everything to be hidden behind modern panels, but the menu bar still matters.

[ALEX]
It does. The menu bar provides the classic structured entry points to commands: File, Edit, Selection, View, Go, Run, Terminal, Help, and related menus depending on platform. For many learners, especially when memorizing shortcuts is still in progress, menus provide a discoverable path.

[JAMIE]
And how do you access it from the keyboard?

[ALEX]
That depends somewhat on platform, but the key idea is that you can reach it without a mouse, open the menus, and arrow through commands. Even if you prefer the Command Palette later, the menu bar remains a valuable backup and discovery tool.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card is: when you don't know the command name yet, menus help you browse the landscape.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's talk about settings sync, because once learners get things accessible, they really don't want to redo it all on every machine.

[ALEX]
That's the big advantage. Settings Sync can carry your configuration across environments. What gets synced can include settings, keybindings, extensions, and related preferences, depending on what you choose to include.

[JAMIE]
How do you enable it?

[ALEX]
Typically through the account and settings flow in VS Code. You sign in, turn on sync, and choose what categories to synchronize. The important idea is intentionality: decide what should travel with you.

[JAMIE]
What about conflicts?

[ALEX]
Sometimes two environments disagree. Conflict resolution is the process of choosing which version wins for a given setting or configuration. Learners should know that sync is powerful, but not magical. If something changes unexpectedly, check whether a synced setting overrode a local one.

[JAMIE]
And then there are profiles, which are almost like named bundles of setup.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Profiles let you create distinct configurations for different contexts. You might have one profile for this workshop, another for general development, and another for experimentation.

[JAMIE]
How do you create one?

[ALEX]
Use the profiles feature in VS Code to create a new profile, give it a meaningful name, and then customize its settings, extensions, and behaviors.

[JAMIE]
And switching profiles?

[ALEX]
You can change from one profile to another through the profiles interface. That allows you to move between setups without manually undoing settings each time.

[JAMIE]
What would you recommend for this workshop?

[ALEX]
A dedicated workshop profile is often a smart move. Keep the accessibility settings, shortcuts, and extensions you need for this class together so you can return to a known-good environment.

[JAMIE]
Can profiles be shared?

[ALEX]
Yes, profiles can be exported and shared, which can be helpful when facilitators want everyone to start from a common baseline or when peers want to compare setups.

[JAMIE]
And how do profiles relate to sync?

[ALEX]
They interact. Settings Sync can preserve and propagate profile-related configuration, but you should still understand which profile you're in and what exactly is being synchronized. The main lesson is: profiles give structure to your setup, and sync helps preserve it.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's open the Settings Editor. A lot of learners know settings exist, but they're not always sure how to work with them accessibly.

[ALEX]
The Settings Editor is the interface for browsing and changing VS Code settings in a more user-friendly way than editing raw JSON by hand. You can open it through menus, commands, or keyboard shortcuts.

[JAMIE]
Once you're inside, what's the best way to navigate?

[ALEX]
Use search. The settings surface can be huge, so searching by concept is often better than browsing endlessly. Type terms like accessibility, screen reader, word wrap, minimap, or sync. Results are grouped and can usually be navigated as structured controls.

[JAMIE]
The source also mentions special search filters.

[ALEX]
Yes. Filters help narrow what you're looking at, such as user versus workspace settings or particular categories. The lesson for learners is that good search plus filters turns settings from overwhelming into manageable.

[JAMIE]
What are the key accessibility settings to configure?

[ALEX]
At minimum, anything related to screen reader support, editor behaviors that affect navigation, and visual complexity settings that may help low-vision users. The exact choices vary by learner, but the chapter's message is clear: configure accessibility intentionally instead of accepting defaults that may not suit your assistive technology.

[JAMIE]
So the learning card would be: search first, filter second, configure deliberately.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
And then we have the Keyboard Shortcuts Editor, which is wonderful if you rely heavily on the keyboard.

[ALEX]
Yes. This editor lets you inspect, search, and customize commands and their shortcuts. It's a central tool for making VS Code fit your hands and workflow.

[JAMIE]
How do you open it?

[ALEX]
Through the command system, menus, or shortcut pathways in VS Code. Once it opens, search is again your friend. Look up commands by name, like Explorer, Command Palette, screen reader mode, settings, or outline.

[JAMIE]
And if a shortcut conflicts with something else or just feels awkward?

[ALEX]
Customize it. That's the beauty of the Keyboard Shortcuts Editor. You can bind a command to a different key combination that better matches your memory, your screen reader conventions, or your physical comfort.

[JAMIE]
That feels especially important for accessibility, because standard shortcuts are not always ideal for every assistive technology setup.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Customization is not indulgence. It can be the difference between friction and fluency.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap, I want to acknowledge something from the table of contents. It points to more advanced topics like essential keyboard navigation, problems, terminal, Copilot Chat, accessible help and accessible diff, accessibility signals, speech, and Git operations inside VS Code.

[ALEX]
Right. Those are important, but this chapter deliberately stays focused on interface and setup. The deep-dive accessibility topics continue in the next chapter. Here, the goal is readiness.

[JAMIE]
And there's even an appendix and source trail for people who want to go deeper.

[ALEX]
Yes. There are related appendices for reference and screen reader support, plus authoritative source links and a section-level source map pointing back to the official docs. That matters because tools evolve, and official documentation is where learners can confirm current behavior.

[JAMIE]
So if we boil today down to a practical checklist, what is it?

[ALEX]
Open VS Code in the simplest way you can, usually github.dev from a repository page. Turn on screen reader mode right away. Open Explorer and prove you can navigate the file tree. Open a file. Use outline or symbols to navigate structure. Open the Command Palette and run a command. Sign in to GitHub and verify the account state. Check whether Copilot is available in your current environment. Learn the major interface regions. Know that the status bar and menu bar are useful, not optional. Use Settings Sync and Profiles to preserve an accessible setup. And remember that the Settings Editor and Keyboard Shortcuts Editor are where VS Code becomes yours.

[JAMIE]
That's a strong foundation.

[ALEX]
It is. And once that foundation is stable, contributing becomes less about wrestling the tool and more about doing the work.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Thanks everyone. If a step didn't work the first time, document it in your evidence comment. That's useful information, not a failure report.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Your accessible development environment is part of your contribution practice. Build it with care, verify it works, and then move forward with confidence.

# VS Code: Interface and Setup

> **Listen to Episode 11:** [VS Code Setup and Accessibility](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview covering both this chapter and [Chapter 12](12-vscode-accessibility.md).

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix G: VS Code Reference](appendix-g-vscode-reference.md) | [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [VS Code Docs: User Interface](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/getstarted/userinterface) | [VS Code Docs: Accessibility](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/accessibility)

## Your Accessible Development Environment - The Foundation

> **Day 2, Block 1 Material**
>
> This chapter covers the VS Code interface: launching VS Code, signing in to GitHub, verifying Copilot is active, configuring screen reader mode, and navigating the Activity Bar, Status Bar, menus, settings, and keyboard shortcuts.
>
> For accessibility deep-dive topics (keyboard navigation, Problems panel, Terminal, Copilot Chat, Accessible Help/View/Diff, Accessibility Signals, and VS Code Speech), see [Chapter 12: VS Code Accessibility Deep Dive](12-vscode-accessibility.md).
>
> **Prerequisites:** Complete Day 1 walkthrough of GitHub's browser interface before working through VS Code material.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 11)

For this workshop, Chapter 11 is a **guided setup chapter** with a lightweight completion practice.

- **Challenge count:** 1 guided walkthrough
- **Automation check:** none - setup state is local/account-level and cannot be validated by the Learning Room PR bot
- **Evidence:** structured completion comment on your assigned challenge issue
- **Pattern:** open, configure, navigate, verify

### Chapter 11 Practice Set

1. **VS Code accessibility baseline** - open VS Code (github.dev or desktop), enable screen reader mode, sign in to GitHub, verify Copilot status, and navigate core surfaces.

### Practice 11.1 Step-by-Step: VS Code Accessibility Baseline

**Goal:** Confirm you can access VS Code (github.dev or desktop), enable screen reader support, sign in to GitHub, check Copilot status, and perform core navigation.

**Where you are working:** github.dev (VS Code in the browser) or desktop VS Code if you installed it in Block 0.

**Estimated time:** 10-15 minutes.

1. Open your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com.
2. Press `.` (the period key) on your keyboard. This launches **github.dev** - a full VS Code editor running in your browser. Wait a few seconds for it to load.
3. Enable screen reader mode:
   - **Windows (NVDA/JAWS):** Press `Shift+Alt+F1`. You should hear an announcement confirming screen reader mode is on.
   - **Mac (VoiceOver):** Screen reader mode is usually already optimized. If navigation feels wrong, open Command Palette (`Cmd+Shift+P`) and run `Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode`.
4. Open the **Explorer** panel with `Ctrl+Shift+E` (Mac: `Cmd+Shift+E`). Your screen reader should announce the file tree.
5. Navigate to and open `README.md` from the file tree. Use arrow keys to move through files and `Enter` to open.
6. Open the **outline/symbols** view with `Ctrl+Shift+O` (Mac: `Cmd+Shift+O`). This shows all headings and sections in the current file - a key navigation tool for screen reader users.
7. Open the **Command Palette** with `Ctrl+Shift+P` (Mac: `Cmd+Shift+P`). Type any command name (for example, `Toggle Word Wrap`) and press `Enter` to run it. Press `Escape` to close without running.
8. Check the **Accounts** button in the Activity Bar (bottom-left of the sidebar). If you are signed in, your screen reader announces your GitHub username. If not, activate it and sign in with GitHub.
9. Check the **Status Bar** at the bottom of the window. Tab or arrow through it to find GitHub Copilot status. If Copilot is active, you hear an indicator showing it is ready.

**You are done when:** You have successfully opened github.dev, enabled screen reader mode, signed in to GitHub, confirmed Copilot status, opened a file, viewed its outline, and run a command from the Command Palette.

### Completing Chapter 11: Submit Your Evidence

Return to GitHub.com, open the assigned setup or Day 2 readiness issue, and post a completion comment:

```text
Chapter 11 completed:
- Opened github.dev: yes / no
- Screen reader mode enabled: yes / no
- Signed in to GitHub: yes / no
- Copilot status checked: yes / no
- Opened file in Explorer: yes / no
- Opened outline/symbols: yes / no
- Opened Command Palette: yes / no
```

If any step was "no," add a note explaining where you got stuck so the facilitator can help. Close the assigned setup or readiness issue when done.

### Expected Outcomes

- Student can launch and navigate github.dev or desktop VS Code.
- Student can enable screen reader mode and hear navigation announcements.
- Student has signed in to GitHub and can see their account status.
- Student has verified GitHub Copilot is active (or knows it requires desktop VS Code).
- Student can open core navigation surfaces (Explorer, Outline, Command Palette).
- Student is ready for VS Code-based contribution chapters (6-16).

### If You Get Stuck

1. Nothing happens when you press `.`? Make sure you are on the repository's main page (not inside an issue or PR). The `.` shortcut only works on repository code pages.
2. Screen reader mode toggle did not announce anything? Open Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and type `Screen Reader` to find the toggle manually.
3. Explorer panel is empty? VS Code may still be loading the repository. Wait 5-10 seconds and press `Ctrl+Shift+E` again.
4. On Mac with VoiceOver, navigation feels wrong? Run `Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode` from Command Palette. VoiceOver sometimes needs the explicit toggle.
5. Cannot find the Accounts button? Open Command Palette and type `Accounts` to manage sign-in from there.
6. Copilot not showing in the status bar? github.dev does not support Copilot - you need desktop VS Code or a Codespace.
7. Shortcut not working? Use Command Palette as a fallback for any action - type what you want to do and VS Code will find the command.
8. Ask facilitator for a side-by-side demo and repeat the same steps.

### Learning Moment

Tool setup is part of contribution skill. A stable, accessible editor reduces stress and increases contribution quality. The surfaces you just tested - github.dev launch, screen reader mode, GitHub sign-in, Copilot status, Explorer, Outline, and Command Palette - are the foundation for everything in Day 2.

1. Open the tool in the simplest way possible (`.` key for github.dev).
2. Sign in and verify your identity and tools are ready (Accounts, Copilot).
3. Configure accessibility before doing any work (screen reader mode first).
4. Verify each navigation surface works with your assistive technology.

### Before you install anything: try VS Code right now in your browser

GitHub provides a web-based version of VS Code called **github.dev**. It runs entirely in your browser with zero installation. The keyboard shortcuts, screen reader mode, and editor experience are identical to the desktop app.

### How to Access github.dev

4. The URL changes to `github.dev/owner/repo`
5. Screen reader mode works exactly as it does in desktop VS Code (toggle with `Shift+Alt+F1`)

#### Where it works

- Repository home pages
- File view pages
- Pull request pages
- Any branch or commit view

**Screen reader note:** The period key shortcut is a single keypress - no modifier keys. It is GitHub's universal "open this in VS Code" command.

**Alternative: Press `>` (Shift+Period)** to open github.dev in a **new tab**. This preserves your GitHub page and is the preferred method when you want to keep both interfaces open.

#### Method 2: Direct URL

Change the domain in any GitHub URL:

- `github.com/owner/repo` becomes `github.dev/owner/repo`
- Works for any branch, file, or commit URL

#### Method 3: From the Repository Page

<details>
<summary>Visual / mouse users</summary>

1. Click the green **Code** button on any repository page
2. In the dropdown, click **Open with github.dev**

</details>

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users (NVDA / JAWS / VoiceOver)</summary>

Everything in the list below works **exactly like desktop VS Code**:

- **Full text editor with syntax highlighting**
- **All VS Code keyboard shortcuts** (see [Section 11: Keyboard Shortcuts Editor](#11-the-keyboard-shortcuts-editor) and [Appendix M](appendix-g-vscode-reference.md#5-complete-keyboard-shortcuts))
- **Screen reader mode** (`Shift+Alt+F1` to activate - Mac: `Shift+Option+F1`)
- **File Explorer** (`Ctrl+Shift+E` - Mac: `Cmd+Shift+E`) - browse the entire repository

- **No terminal** - cannot run shell commands, npm, git CLI

- **No live server or preview** - except Markdown preview, which does work

## 3. Screen Reader Mode in VS Code

> **See also:** [Chapter 12: VS Code Accessibility](12-vscode-accessibility.md) goes deeper into accessibility features, Accessible View, and signal customization.

> **Who needs this section?** If you use NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, or another screen reader, read this section before continuing. If you are not using a screen reader, you can skip to [Section 4](#4-the-vs-code-interface-tour) - VS Code works fully without enabling this mode.

VS Code has built-in accessibility support designed for screen reader users. It changes how focus moves, how announcements work, and how navigation behaves.

### Activating Screen Reader Mode

| Method | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Keyboard shortcut | `Shift+Alt+F1` (Windows) / `Shift+Option+F1` (Mac) |
| Command Palette | `Ctrl+Shift+P` (Windows) / `Cmd+Shift+P` (Mac) then type "screen reader" then select "Toggle Screen Reader Accessibility Mode" |
| Auto-detection | VS Code detects NVDA and JAWS automatically on Windows; VoiceOver on macOS |

#### Verify it is active

Open Settings (`Ctrl+,` - Mac: `Cmd+,`) then search for `accessibility support` then confirm it shows `on` (not `auto`).

### What Changes in Screen Reader Mode

| Area | Normal Mode | Screen Reader Mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suggestions list | Popup overlay | Announced via ARIA live region |
| Diff navigation | Visual highlighting | Announces "Added" / "Removed" before line content |
| Error indicators | Red underlines | Announced on focus |
| Inline decorations | Displayed visually | Suppressed to reduce noise |
| Tab completion | Visual ghost text | Announced as suggestion |

### NVDA-Specific Settings for VS Code

VS Code uses a web-based renderer. Configure NVDA for best results:

1. Open NVDA Menu then Preferences then Settings then Browse Mode
2. Set "Maximum length of text on a single line" to `10000` (prevents truncation in long lines)
3. Under Object Presentation: set "Report tooltip delay" to `off`
4. Recommended: use **NVDA + Google Chrome** for the integrated browser panels

### JAWS-Specific Settings for VS Code

1. JAWS should detect VS Code automatically and switch to PC Cursor mode for the editor
2. If the editor feels unresponsive, press `Insert+Z` to toggle virtual cursor off
3. For the integrated terminal: use `Insert+Z` to enter forms/PC mode, then interact with the terminal

### VoiceOver-Specific Settings for VS Code (macOS)

1. Open VS Code then `Shift+Alt+F1` (Mac: `Shift+Option+F1`) to confirm screen reader mode
2. In VoiceOver Utility: Verbosity then set "Punctuation" to "All" for reading code
3. Use Quick Nav OFF (`Left+Right Arrow`) when inside the editor - standard cursor navigation is more predictable
4. Use `VO+Shift+Down` to interact with the editor, `VO+Shift+Up` to stop interacting

- Toggle screen reader mode with `Shift+Alt+F1` (Mac: `Shift+Option+F1`) -- VS Code announces "Screen reader optimized" when activated
- Set `editor.accessibilitySupport` to `"on"` (not `"auto"`) in Settings (`Ctrl+,`) for consistent behavior across sessions
- NVDA users: set "Maximum length of text on a single line" to 10000 in Browse Mode settings to prevent long code lines from being truncated

## 4. The VS Code Interface Tour

Before diving into individual features, here is how VS Code is organized. Every area is reachable by keyboard.

### The Five Major Regions

```text
+----------------------------------------------------------+
|  Menu Bar (File, Edit, View, Go, Run, Terminal, Help)    |
+------+---------------------------------------------------+
|      |                                                    |
| A    |  Editor Area                                       |
| c    |  (your files open here)                            |
| t    |                                                    |
| i    |                                                    |
| v    |                                                    |
| i    +---------------------------------------------------+
| t    |                                                    |
| y    |  Panel (Terminal, Problems, Output, Debug Console) |
|      |                                                    |
| B    +---------------------------------------------------+
| a    |  Status Bar (line, column, language, Git branch,   |
| r    |   Copilot status, encoding, notifications)         |
+------+---------------------------------------------------+
```

**Text description of the layout above:** VS Code has five major regions arranged in a grid. The **Menu Bar** spans the full width across the top. Below it, the **Activity Bar** runs vertically along the left edge (it contains icons for Explorer, Source Control, Search, Extensions, and more). The **Sidebar** appears to the right of the Activity Bar and shows content for the selected activity (file tree, search results, etc.). The **Editor Area** fills the large central region where your files open. Below the Editor Area, the **Panel** stretches across the bottom and contains the Terminal, Problems, Output, and Debug Console tabs. Finally, the **Status Bar** runs along the very bottom showing line number, column, language mode, Git branch, Copilot status, encoding, and notifications.

### Navigating Between Regions

| Region | Keyboard Shortcut | What You Hear (Screen Reader) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activity Bar icons | `Ctrl+Shift+E` / `G` / `F` / `X` / etc. | "Explorer", "Source Control", etc. |
| Sidebar content | Follows activity bar selection | Tree view or list content |
| Editor area | `Ctrl+1` (first editor group) | File name and cursor position |
| Panel | `Ctrl+Backtick` (terminal) or `Ctrl+Shift+M` (problems) | Panel name announcement |
| Status Bar | `F6` cycles through regions | Status bar items read left to right |

**Key insight:** Press `F6` repeatedly to cycle focus through the major regions: Sidebar, Editor, Panel, Status Bar, and back. This is the universal "where am I, take me somewhere else" key in VS Code.

## 6. Verifying GitHub Copilot Status

GitHub Copilot is your AI pair programmer. Before starting any contribution work, confirm it is active and responding.

### Where to Check Copilot Status

#### Status Bar Indicator

The Copilot icon appears in the **Status Bar** at the bottom-right of the VS Code window.

| Icon State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Copilot icon (normal) | Copilot is active and ready |
| Copilot icon with warning triangle | Copilot has a configuration issue |
| Copilot icon with slash-through | Copilot is disabled for this file type |
| No Copilot icon | Extension not installed or not signed in |

#### Command Palette Check

1. Press `Ctrl+Shift+P`
2. Type `GitHub Copilot: Status`
3. The output shows whether Copilot is signed in, active, or has errors

#### Quick Test

1. Open any `.md` file in the editor
2. Start typing a sentence (for example, `## Getting Started with`)
3. If Copilot is active, a gray ghost-text suggestion appears after a brief pause
4. Press `Tab` to accept or `Escape` to dismiss

### Troubleshooting Copilot

| Problem | Solution |
| --- | --- |
| No Copilot icon in status bar | On VS Code 1.116+, Copilot is built-in -- sign in to GitHub (`Ctrl+Shift+P` then `GitHub: Sign in`). On older VS Code: `Ctrl+Shift+X` then search `GitHub Copilot` then install |
| Icon shows warning | Open Output panel (`Ctrl+Shift+U`), select "GitHub Copilot" from the dropdown, read the error |
| "Not signed in" | Sign in to GitHub (Section 5 above) |
| Copilot not suggesting | Check that Copilot is not disabled for the file type: `Ctrl+Shift+P` then `GitHub Copilot: Toggle` |
| Works on desktop but not github.dev | Expected behavior. github.dev does not support Copilot. Use desktop VS Code or a Codespace. |

## 9. Settings Sync

**Settings Sync** synchronizes your VS Code configuration across multiple machines and between desktop VS Code and github.dev. When you sign in and enable sync, your settings, keyboard shortcuts, extensions, UI state, and profiles travel with you.

### What Gets Synced

| Category | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Settings | `editor.fontSize`, `editor.accessibilitySupport`, color theme, zoom level |
| Keyboard Shortcuts | All custom keybindings |
| Extensions | Installed extensions list |
| UI State | Sidebar position, panel visibility, recent files |
| Profiles | Named collections of settings for different workflows |

### Enabling Settings Sync

1. Open the **Accounts** button (Activity Bar, bottom-left) or press `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type `Settings Sync: Turn On`
2. Sign in with your GitHub account (or Microsoft account)
3. Select which categories to sync (recommended: sync everything)
4. VS Code syncs immediately and on every subsequent change

### Conflict Resolution

If settings differ between machines, VS Code shows a merge editor where you choose which version to keep. This is similar to a Git merge conflict but for settings.

### Learning Cards: Settings Sync

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- After enabling sync, all your accessibility settings (screen reader mode, accessibility signals, minimap disabled) apply on every machine
- Changes sync automatically in the background - no manual action needed after initial setup
- If a conflict occurs, VS Code opens a merge editor that is navigable with standard diff commands (F7 / Shift+F7)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Your zoom level, font size, and High Contrast theme sync across machines
- After initial setup on one machine, every other VS Code instance immediately gets the same visual configuration
- Use Profiles to maintain separate configurations (e.g., "Presentation" profile with extra-large fonts)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- The sync status appears as a circular arrow icon in the Activity Bar (bottom-left, near Accounts)
- Conflicts and sync status are shown via notification banners
- Use `Ctrl+Shift+P` then "Settings Sync: Show Synced Data" to review what was synchronized

</details>

### Profiles

VS Code **Profiles** let you create named collections of settings, extensions, keyboard shortcuts, snippets, tasks, and UI state. Each profile is independent - switching profiles changes your entire VS Code configuration instantly. This is useful when you work in different contexts (workshop vs. daily development) or need to present with different display settings.

#### Creating a Profile

| Method | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Command Palette | `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type `Profiles: Create Profile` |
| Gear menu | Click the gear icon (bottom-left of Activity Bar) then `Profiles` then `Create Profile` |

When creating a profile, you choose what to include:

- **Settings** - editor preferences, accessibility options, theme
- **Keyboard Shortcuts** - all custom keybindings
- **Extensions** - which extensions are installed and enabled
- **Snippets** - code snippet definitions
- **Tasks** - task runner configurations
- **UI State** - sidebar position, panel layout, view visibility

You can start from the current configuration, an empty profile, or an existing profile template.

#### Switching Profiles

| Method | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| Command Palette | `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type `Profiles: Switch Profile` |
| Gear menu | Click the gear icon then `Profiles` then select a profile name |
| Status Bar | The current profile name appears in the Status Bar when you are not using the Default profile - click it to switch |

The active profile name appears in the VS Code title bar and Status Bar so you always know which configuration is active.

#### Workshop Profile Recommendations

Create these profiles before the workshop:

| Profile Name | Purpose | Key Settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workshop** | Accessibility-optimized for this event | Screen reader mode on, accessibility signals enabled, minimap off, word wrap on (see the [Recommended Workshop Profile](#recommended-workshop-profile) settings in Section 17) |
| **Presentation** | Large fonts for demos or shared screens | `editor.fontSize: 24`, `terminal.integrated.fontSize: 20`, `window.zoomLevel: 2`, High Contrast theme |
| **Default** | Your everyday development settings | Whatever you normally use |

#### Exporting and Sharing Profiles

Profiles can be exported and shared:

1. `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type `Profiles: Export Profile`
2. Choose what to include (settings, extensions, etc.)
3. Export as a **GitHub gist** (shareable link) or a **local file**
4. Share the link or file with others

To import: `Ctrl+Shift+P` then `Profiles: Import Profile` and paste the gist URL or select the file.

**Workshop tip:** Facilitators can export a pre-configured Workshop profile as a GitHub gist and share the link. Students import it in one step and immediately have all accessibility settings configured.

#### Profiles and Settings Sync

Profiles sync across machines through Settings Sync. When you create a profile on one machine and have Settings Sync enabled, the profile appears on every other machine where you are signed in. Each profile syncs independently - changes to one profile do not affect others.

## 10. The Settings Editor

The Settings Editor is where you customize VS Code. There are two views: the graphical settings UI and the raw `settings.json` file.

### Opening the Settings Editor

| Method | Shortcut |
| --- | --- |
| Graphical Settings UI | `Ctrl+,` (Mac: `Cmd+,`) |
| JSON Settings file | `Ctrl+Shift+P` then type "Open User Settings (JSON)" |

### Navigating the Settings Editor

The graphical Settings UI has a **search box** at the top. Type any keyword and the settings list filters instantly.

#### Special Search Filters

| Filter | What It Shows |
| --- | --- |
| `@modified` | Only settings you have changed from their defaults |
| `@tag:accessibility` | All accessibility-related settings |
| `@tag:advanced` | Advanced, less commonly used settings |
| `@tag:experimental` | Experimental features not yet enabled by default |
| `@ext:github.copilot` | Settings for the GitHub Copilot extension |

### Key Accessibility Settings to Configure

```json
{
  "editor.accessibilitySupport": "on",
  "editor.minimap.enabled": false,
  "editor.wordWrap": "on",
  "editor.renderWhitespace": "none",
  "editor.fontSize": 16,
  "accessibility.signals.lineHasError": "on",
  "accessibility.signals.taskCompleted": "on",
  "accessibility.signals.chatResponseReceived": "on"
}
```

### Learning Cards: Settings Editor

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Press `Ctrl+,` to open Settings. Focus lands in the search box - start typing immediately

The Keyboard Shortcuts Editor lets you view, search, and customize every keyboard shortcut in VS Code.

The editor has a search box that supports:
